patches.old: If the left side has more moles, Q increases → reverse shift. If the right side has more moles, Q decreases → forward shift.
patches.new: Compressing multiplies every concentration by the same factor f, so Q changes by f^Δn. If the *left* side has more moles of gas (Δn < 0), Q **decreases** → forward shift, toward the side with fewer moles. If the *right* side has more moles (Δn > 0), Q **increases** → reverse shift. Either way the system moves toward the side with fewer gas molecules, which is what relieves the pressure — and it is why the Haber process is run at high pressure to favour NH₃.
patches.reason: Both halves were inverted. Squeezing the Haber mixture (4 mol of gas on the left, 2 on the right) shifts it *toward* ammonia — that is the entire industrial reason for running it at high pressure — but the rule as printed predicts a reverse shift. Formally Q scales as f^Δn, so a negative Δn makes Q fall, not rise. Compression always drives a system toward the side with fewer moles of gas, and the corrected sentence now says so explicitly as the check.

patches.old: If K_a << C (specifically, if C/K_a > 100), the small-x approximation applies:
patches.new: If K_a << C (specifically, if C/K_a > 400), the small-x approximation applies:
patches.reason: C/Ka > 100 fails this lesson's own 5% rule, stated two paragraphs earlier. Since x ≈ √(Ka·C), the fractional dissociation is x/C = √(Ka/C); a ratio of 100 gives √(1/100) = 10%, double the allowed error. The threshold that actually satisfies 5% is C/Ka > 400, which is also the figure the weak-acid lesson in this course uses (acetic acid's 5% cutoff at ≈7 mM = 400 × 1.8 × 10⁻⁵).

patches.old: - Water: pK_a = 15.7 (sometimes listed as 14 in certain contexts)
patches.new: - Water: pK_a = 14 when water is the solvent being deprotonated — which is the convention in use everywhere else on this list, and the one that makes K_a × K_b = K_w come out right. (15.7 is the organic-chemistry convention, which treats water as a 55.5 M solute; the two differ by a factor of about 55, so never mix them in one problem.)
patches.reason: The emphasis is inverted relative to the acid-base lesson in this course, which establishes that 14 is the value to use when water is the solvent and reserves 15.7 for the organic convention. It matters here in particular, because this list sits beside Ka × Kb = Kw and the acetate Kb calculation, both of which only work with pKa 14 — using 15.7 there is what produces the factor-of-55 error that lesson corrects.

The denominator is (0.50)(0.50)³ = (0.50)(0.125) = 0.0625, not 0.03125 — the printed value is 0.50⁵, one factor of 0.50 too many. Q is therefore 4.0, not 8.0. The answer and the direction of shift are unaffected, but a student who reproduces the arithmetic gets 4.0 and will assume the mistake is theirs.

patches.old: A student sets up an ICE table for the reaction A(g) ⇌ 2B(g) with Kc = 4.0.
patches.new: A student sets up an ICE table for the reaction A(g) ⇌ 2B(g) with Kc = 2.0.
patches.reason: With Kc = 4.0 the stated solution x = 0.50 M is impossible: (2x)²/(1−x) = 4.0 gives x = 0.618. The question only tests that [B] = 2x, so the inconsistency does not change the key — but a student who checks the stem against Kc finds it does not close. Kc = 2.0 makes x = 0.50 exact: (1.0)²/(0.50) = 2.0.

sources.title: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e — 13.3 Shifting Equilibria: Le Châtelier's Principle
sources.note: A system at equilibrium responds to a stress in the direction that partially relieves it. For a gas-phase reaction, reducing the volume (raising the pressure) shifts the equilibrium toward the side with the smaller number of moles of gas; a temperature change is the only stress that alters K itself.

sources.title: Chemistry LibreTexts (OpenStax Chemistry 2e) — 13.2 Equilibrium Constants
sources.note: Q has the same form as K but is evaluated at any composition; Q < K shifts the reaction right and Q > K shifts it left. Worked examples of predicting the direction of shift, and the omission of pure solids and liquids from both expressions.

visual.title: Q first, then the ICE table
visual.alt: A five-step workflow: write the balanced equation and the equilibrium expression excluding pure solids and liquids; compute Q from the values given; compare Q with K, which fixes the direction and therefore the sign of x; build the initial, change and equilibrium rows; solve and substitute back to check. A second panel gives the three ways to solve and says to choose before expanding — take the square root of the whole expression when both sides are perfect squares, drop x from the denominator when the initial concentration exceeds four hundred times K, and otherwise use the quadratic. A worked table runs hydrogen plus iodine to hydrogen iodide at K equals 49, with initial values 1.00, 1.00 and zero, changes of minus x, minus x and plus 2x, and the square-root shortcut giving x equal to 0.778 and hydrogen iodide at 1.56 molar, verified at 49.1. A further panel shows the sign of x flipping with Q: below K the reaction runs forward so reactants take minus x and products plus x, above K it runs backward so the signs reverse. A footer derives the condition for dropping x — five per cent of the initial concentration means the concentration must exceed four hundred times K, not one hundred, since a ratio of one hundred gives a ten per cent error — worked on acetic acid, fine at 0.10 molar and invalid at 0.0010 molar. A final note records that products present at the start change only the initial row, and that a pure solid or liquid has no row at all.
visual.caption: The direction comes from Q, and the direction is what sets the sign of x. Decide that before drawing the table, not after.
